title: Running, four soundtracks
introduction:
This piece comprises an image and four audio tracks. Track A closely follows the image, striving for a faithful reproduction on a physical level; Track B completely ignores the image; Track C partially follows the image; whilst Track D creates a contrast with the image.

I selected the ‘Running Stick Figure’ I created in the second week as my source material. As this is my own original work, I was able to use it directly, thereby devoting more time and energy to sound design. This concept stemmed from Miguel Mera’s lecture this week: the same image can evoke entirely different feelings when accompanied by different soundtracks. The three levels of synchronisation he proposed (derived from Kevin Donnelly) inspired me to create Tracks A, B and C, whilst I added Track D, a track that runs counter to the direction of the image.

Initially, when the Week 2 project ran as is, the results were not ideal. It was too short and the effect was rather weak. So I adjusted the parameters: I extended the canvas length, increased the speed of the legs in the middle section to four times the original, and smoothed out the motion path, as if climbing a gentle slope and then gliding down slowly.
related_work:
Before this week, I read Walter Murch. I believe he put forward three rules. Firstly, re- association: you can attribute a particular sound to something that cannot produce it, such as having a person imitate a bird’s call. Secondly, when sound and image do not match, a metaphor is formed; every successful re-association is a metaphor, and every metaphor initially appears to be a mistake. Third, the greater the discrepancy, the more room there is for the audience to exercise their imagination; however, if the discrepancy is too great, people will be unable to comprehend it [1][2].

During his lecture, Miguel Mera discussed the concept of ‘synchresis’ proposed by Michel Chion: when sound and action occur simultaneously, the brain fuses them together, even if there is no logical connection whatsoever [3]. He also illustrated the three levels proposed by Kevin Donnelly: tight synchronisation, near-synchronisation (almost synchronous) and asynchrony [4]. A cartoon example is ‘Mickey Mousing’, where the music follows every movement of the character. My Track A employs ‘Mickey Mousing’ for the stick figure character; as the stick figure is itself a cartoon character, it does not appear comical.
method:
All sounds were generated by code; I did not download anything. The footsteps consist of a series of short noise pulses combined with a low, muffled thud, whilst the breathing sounds are filtered noise shaped to resemble inhalation and exhalation. The timing of the footsteps is derived from the running code itself, so every ‘thud’ on Track A represents a real step: 98 steps in total for one lap.

Track A (tight sync, physical): Each time a real foot strikes the ground, there is a click; the breathing rhythm quickens in time with the leg movements. The strides are longer at both ends, so each footfall is heavy; in the middle section, the strides are shorter and the footfalls are lighter. The camera remains stationary, so the sound moves from the left ear to the right, reaching its loudest point when the runner passes the centre.

Track B (Asynchronous): A fixed beat of 1.5 clicks per second, with steady and consistent breathing.

Track C (Near-Synchronous): Every step is present, but each click is delayed by 0.1 to 0.3 seconds, and approximately one step is omitted every five steps. Although the breathing is synchronised with the footage, the response is sluggish.

Audio Track D (Contrapuntal): The opposite of the visuals. The legs running fast are accompanied by sparse tapping sounds and steady breathing; the legs running slowly are accompanied by dense tapping sounds and laboured breathing.

Only the audio track name is displayed in the top right-hand corner of each clip. There are no other subtitles: I want the audience to focus on the stick figure, rather than reading text.

To clarify our respective responsibilities. The creative direction stemmed from that lecture: a single image with multiple audio tracks, each of which alters the sensation of running. I incorporated this concept into this week’s work plan and asked the AI whether it was feasible and met the creative requirements; the AI agreed and helped me establish the overall framework. I then produced the image and audio track A: I identified the characteristic sounds of real running (heavy footsteps at the beginning and end of a stride, light footsteps in the middle, louder sounds as the runner passes the centre, and the sound moving from the left ear to the right ear), and personally adjusted the relevant parameters until it felt just right, making the

footsteps at the beginning and end heavier than in the initial version, and the sounds in the middle louder than in the initial version. The remaining three synchronisation-level audio tracks B, C and D were generated by the AI based on relationship rules I specified: ignore the visuals, partially follow the visuals, and contrast with the visuals. The sound synthesis and recording scripts were also AI-generated code; the running code and its four lines of modifications were written by me.
results_discussion:
To be honest, the changes that C and D brought to the visuals weren’t as significant as I’d expected. They mainly made one feel uncomfortable. If ranked by how uncomfortable they are, B comes last: it’s the most awkward one. Although the rhythm is still there, it has absolutely no connection to the visuals, so the two never quite gel. D, on the other hand, runs completely counter to the visuals, but it has its own internal logic, so it’s actually quite watchable. Option C feels like a slip-up, much like a film with poor dubbing, though one gets used to it after a few seconds.

Therefore, it is not the segment that contradicts the visuals that feels jarring, but rather the one that bears absolutely no relation to them. This aligns perfectly with Murch’s view: a metaphor may initially appear to be a mistake, yet one can still grasp its meaning. Option B, however, is not a metaphor; it is simply a mistake.
conclusion_future_work:
The video below plays four audio tracks in sequence (A, B, C and D, totalling 100 seconds). The image shows the sparsely, moderately and most densely populated sections of the piece during this run, the four lines of code I have modified, and the loudness curves for the four audio tracks. If this piece is included in the final collection, the next step will be to create a web-based version,

allowing viewers to switch between the four audio tracks whilst the same image continues to play.
